1.tip: The CLIENT talks by broadcast: DISCOVER and REQUEST. The server's OFFER and ACK are its replies.
1.why: When the client boots it has no IP address and doesn't know the server, so it broadcasts DISCOVER. It broadcasts REQUEST too, so every server that made an offer hears which one it picked.

2.tip: ip ADDRESS dhcp = this interface GETS an address. ip dhcp POOL = the router GIVES addresses.
2.why: The ip address dhcp command on an interface turns the router into a DHCP client on that port, so it asks a DHCPv4 server for its address, mask and other settings.

3.cue: why is the DHCPREQUEST message sent as a broadcast
3.tip: One broadcast REQUEST = 'yes' to one server and 'no thanks' to all the others at once.
3.why: Several DHCP servers may have sent offers. Broadcasting the REQUEST lets all of them see which offer the client accepted, so the others can put their offered addresses back in their pools.

4.tip: All zeros = the client knows nothing yet. That's the very first message: DISCOVER.
4.why: Before DISCOVER the client has no address, mask or gateway, so all are 0.0.0.0, and it doesn't know any server, so it sends to the broadcast address 255.255.255.255.

5.cue: automates assignment of IP addresses, port number
5.tip: DHCP server listens on 67, client on 68. DNS is 53, HTTP is 80.
5.why: DHCP hands out IP addresses automatically. The DHCP server listens on UDP port 67. DNS (port 53) turns names into addresses, it doesn't assign them.

6.cue: PC1 has been shut down for two weeks
6.tip: Lease gone = start over from scratch = broadcast to 255.255.255.255.
6.why: After two weeks the old lease has expired, so PC1 starts fresh with a DISCOVER. It doesn't know the server yet, so it sends to the limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255.

7.cue: reply when it receives a DHCPOFFER
7.tip: D-O-R-A: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. After Offer comes Request.
7.why: When the client gets an OFFER it answers with a REQUEST that says 'I'd like that address, please'. The server then confirms with an ACK.

8.cue: acquire an IPv4 address automatically from an ISP
8.tip: You want an ADDRESS from DHCP: ip address dhcp. helper-address relays, pool serves.
8.why: Typed on the interface facing the ISP, ip address dhcp makes the router a DHCP client so the ISP gives it an address. ip helper-address only relays requests for others.

9.tip: Renewing? The client already knows its server, so it sends a unicast REQUEST straight to it.
9.why: To keep its lease the client sends a DHCPREQUEST directly (unicast) to the server that gave it the address, because it already knows that server's IP address.

10.cue: let the client know it is able to use the provided IP
10.tip: ACK = acknowledged: 'Yes, it's yours'. NAK = 'No, you can't have it'.
10.why: The DHCPACK is the server's final confirmation. Once the client gets it, it can start using the IP address, mask, gateway and DNS settings it was given.

11.cue: Windows computer did not receive an IPv4 address
11.tip: 169.254 = 'I got nothing from DHCP'. Windows gives itself an APIPA address.
11.why: If no DHCP server answers, Windows assigns itself an APIPA address from 169.254.0.0/16. Seeing 169.254 means DHCP failed. The loopback 127.0.0.1 still works.

12.cue: client send to accept an IPv4 address
12.tip: The client ACCEPTS with a REQUEST, and it's a broadcast so the other servers hear too.
12.why: The client accepts an offer by sending a DHCPREQUEST. It is broadcast so any other servers that made offers learn they weren't chosen. ACK comes from the server, not the client.

13.cue: coffee shop wireless router and a DSL modem
13.tip: The ISP is the DHCP server. The router's WAN port is its client.
13.why: The phone company (ISP) gives out the public address. Setting the router's WAN side as a DHCP client lets it get that address automatically, while the router serves the inside network.

14.cue: Which two UDP ports are used to forward DHCP
14.tip: 6-7 server, 6-8 client. DHCP lives at 67 and 68.
14.why: DHCP uses UDP port 67 for the server and UDP port 68 for the client. Relay agents forward traffic between those ports. Port 53 is DNS and 23 is Telnet.

15.cue: How will a client device obtain a usable IP address
15.tip: First step is always DISCOVER, and it's a broadcast: MAC FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF.
15.why: The client starts with no address and no server info, so it sends a DHCPDISCOVER to the Layer 2 broadcast MAC FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF so every device on the segment receives it.

16.cue: advantage of configuring a Cisco router as a relay agent
16.tip: ip helper-address helps MORE than DHCP: it relays several UDP services like DNS and TFTP too.
16.why: The ip helper-address command forwards several UDP broadcast services by default (DHCP, DNS, TFTP and others), not just DHCP. It doesn't make the server faster or forward multicasts.

17.cue: Which statement is true about DHCP operation
17.tip: Boot up = shout out. The client broadcasts DISCOVER to find any server.
17.why: A new DHCP client doesn't know any server, so it broadcasts DISCOVER to find one. The REQUEST is broadcast, not unicast, and DISCOVER carries no address info.

18.why: The client discovers a server, the server offers an address, the client requests that address, and the server acknowledges it. That's the four-step DHCP lease process.

19.cue: M flag as 0 and O flag as 1

keys.k: information that is contained in the RA message and contact a DHCPv6 server

19.tip: O = Other info. M=0, O=1 is stateless DHCPv6: address from the RA, extras like DNS from DHCPv6.
19.why: With M off and O on, the PC builds its own address from the prefix in the RA (SLAAC) and then asks a DHCPv6 server only for other info, such as DNS. That's stateless DHCPv6.

20.cue: allow PC-A to receive an IPv6 address from the DHCPv6 server
20.tip: Put the relay on the interface that faces the CLIENTS, not the server.
20.why: PC-A's DHCPv6 messages stay on its own link. The relay command goes on the router interface where PC-A's requests arrive, Fa0/0, so the router can forward them to the server on the other network.

21.cue: clients are not getting the DNS server address
21.tip: No O flag = plain SLAAC: hosts get the prefix but never ask DHCPv6 for DNS.
21.why: The interface is missing ipv6 nd other-config-flag, so RAs tell hosts to use SLAAC only. They make their own addresses but never contact the DHCPv6 server for DNS and domain name.

22.tip: IPv6 hosts point to the router's link-local (FE80) address as their gateway.
22.why: Router advertisements are sent from the router's link-local address, so SLAAC hosts use that FE80 address as their default gateway, not the global address.

23.cue: configuring a router for DHCPv6 operation, commands
23.tip: Pool has DNS and domain name but no address range + other-config-flag = stateless.
23.why: The pool only gives DNS and domain name info, with no address prefix, and the interface uses the other-config-flag. Hosts make their own addresses, so it is stateless DHCPv6.

24.cue: feature that is associated with HSRP
24.tip: HSRP: Hot Standby. One active router, one standby waiting.
24.why: HSRP is Cisco's protocol where one router is active and forwards traffic, while a standby router waits to take over. It's proprietary and doesn't load balance (that's GLBP).

25.cue: load balanced across the two gateways
25.tip: GLBP: Gateway Load Balancing Protocol. Load balancing is in the name.
25.why: GLBP lets several gateway routers share the traffic at the same time while still backing each other up. STP and PVST+ are Layer 2 loop prevention protocols, not gateway protocols.

26.cue: Which IPv4 gateway address should be configured on the host
26.tip: With an FHRP, hosts use the VIRTUAL IP, not either real router's address.
26.why: The FHRP routers share a virtual IP address, here 192.168.2.100. Hosts use it as their gateway so they keep working if one router fails. .1 and .2 are the real routers.

27.cue: Which destination MAC address, default gateway
27.tip: Virtual IP goes with a virtual MAC. Hosts never need to know which real router is working.
27.why: With an FHRP, hosts send frames to the virtual router's MAC address. Whichever router is active answers for that MAC, so a failover doesn't change anything on the hosts.

28.tip: Cisco + load sharing + IPv4 = GLBP. Add 'for IPv6' only when the question says IPv6.
28.why: GLBP is Cisco's FHRP that shares traffic across several routers. The question says IPv4, so plain GLBP is right, not GLBP for IPv6. VRRP and IRDP are open standards.

29.why: A /25 has 128 addresses. Take away the network and broadcast addresses for 126 usable hosts. Reserving 8 for servers leaves 118 in the pool.

30.cue: verify that the address is unique
30.tip: DAD: Duplicate Address Detection. Ask with NS, and silence (no NA) means it's free.
30.why: IPv6 uses Duplicate Address Detection: the host sends a neighbor solicitation for its own new address. If no neighbor advertisement comes back, nobody else has it. IPv6 has no ARP.

keys.k: active device and a standby device

31.tip: HSRP says ACTIVE and STANDBY. VRRP says MASTER and BACKUP.
31.why: HSRP picks one active router to be the gateway and one standby to take over if it fails. The 'master' wording is VRRP, and the ICMP option describes IRDP.

32.why: DHCP follows DORA: the client sends Discover to find a server, the server sends an Offer, the client sends Request to accept it, and the server confirms with Ack.

33.cue: Match the purpose with its DHCP message type

keys.k: DHCPDISCOVER A message that is used to locate
DHCPOFFER A message that is used to suggest
DHCPREQUEST A message that is used to identify the explicit server
DHCPACK A message is used by a server to finalize

33.tip: Discover = find, Offer = suggest, Request = pick, Ack = finalize.
33.why: DISCOVER finds servers, OFFER suggests a lease, REQUEST names the server and offer the client wants, and the server's ACK finalizes the lease. NAK is the unused option.

34.tip: SARR: Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply. It's DORA for IPv6.
34.why: The client solicits for servers, a server advertises itself, the client requests an address, and the server replies with it. It mirrors the IPv4 Discover, Offer, Request, Ack steps.

keys.k: Step 2 The standby router stops seeing hello
Step 3 The standby router assumes the role
Step 4 The new forwarding router assumes both

35.tip: Fail, silence, take over, take the addresses.
35.why: The active router fails, so its hello messages stop. The standby notices, becomes the forwarding router, and takes over the virtual IP and MAC so hosts keep the same gateway.

keys.k: HSRP A Cisco proprietary FHRP that provides redundancy through use of an active
GLBP A Cisco proprietary FHRP that provides load sharing

36.tip: HSRP = active/standby, VRRP = open standard master/backup, GLBP = load balancing.
36.why: HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-only. HSRP uses an active and standby router, GLBP also shares the load. VRRP is the open standard and calls its routers master and backup.

37.why: The client discovers servers, a server offers an address, the client requests it, and the server acknowledges. Then the client can use the address.

38.why: A /27 has 32 addresses. Minus network and broadcast leaves 30 usable. Reserving 22 for IP phones leaves 8 for other hosts.

39.cue: lease duration 5 days, absence of one week
39.tip: Expired lease = start over. Broadcast at both layers: all F's MAC, all 255s IP.
39.why: After a week the 5-day lease has expired, so the PC starts with a DISCOVER. It doesn't know the server, so it uses broadcast addresses at both Layer 2 and Layer 3.

40.cue: IP address that is assigned to a particular MAC
40.tip: BINDING ties a MAC to an IP. Pool shows totals, statistics shows message counts.
40.why: show ip dhcp binding lists each leased IP address with the MAC address (hardware address) of the client that has it, plus the lease end time.

41.cue: ISP commonly assigns a DHCP address to a wireless router
41.tip: DHCP = no manual typing. The ISP manages thousands of customers easily.
41.why: With DHCP the ISP doesn't have to set each customer's address by hand. It can hand out, change and reuse addresses automatically, which makes managing them easy.

42.tip: Binding = who got what: IP addresses assigned to hosts.
42.why: The binding table shows which IPv4 addresses the DHCP server has leased to which hosts. Excluded addresses are in the running config, and pool counts are in show ip dhcp pool.

43.tip: Two addresses = a RANGE. From .1 to .15 is 15 addresses.
43.why: Giving two addresses to excluded-address marks the whole range from the first to the last, so .1 through .15, 15 addresses, will never be leased to clients.

44.cue: Match the descriptions to the corresponding DHCPv6 server type

keys.k: M flag is set to 1 in RA messages Stateful
INFORMATION REQUEST messages to the server Stateless

44.tip: Stateful = M flag, address pool, ipv6 address dhcp. Stateless = O flag, INFORMATION REQUEST, autoconfig.
44.why: In stateful DHCPv6 the server hands out addresses (M flag, address pool, ipv6 address dhcp). In stateless the host makes its own address and only asks for extra info (O flag, autoconfig).

45.cue: what kind of IPv6 addressing is being configured
45.tip: Address from SLAAC + DNS from a DHCPv6 server = stateless DHCPv6.
45.why: The output shows the host building its own address from the RA while also getting extra info like DNS from a DHCPv6 server. That mix is stateless DHCPv6.

46.tip: Cisco + load balancing + IPv6 = GLBP for IPv6.
46.why: GLBP is Cisco's load balancing FHRP, and the IPv6 version is GLBP for IPv6. VRRP versions are open standards, and VRRPv2 is IPv4 only.

47.tip: A /23 ends at 101.255, so the last usable is 101.254. Pool commands: network and default-router, no 'ip'.
47.why: The first 10 are .100.1 to .100.10, and a /23 runs to 192.168.101.255, so the last host is 101.254. Inside the pool the right commands are network with mask 255.255.254.0 and default-router.

48.why: When no DHCP server answers, hosts give themselves an APIPA link-local address from 169.254.0.0/16. They can only talk to other hosts on the same link.

49.cue: workstations did not obtain the correct prefix
49.tip: No ipv6 unicast-routing = no RAs. The router won't act like an IPv6 router.
49.why: A Cisco router only sends router advertisements (with the prefix and length) after ipv6 unicast-routing is turned on. Without RAs, SLAAC hosts can't learn the prefix.

50.tip: IRDP: ICMP Router Discovery Protocol. ICMP is right in the name.
50.why: IRDP is an older open standard that uses ICMP router advertisements and solicitations so hosts can find a working gateway. GLBP is Cisco-only and VRRP doesn't use ICMP.

51.cue: PC-A is unable to receive an IPv6 address from the stateful
51.tip: The relay listens where the client talks. Put it on the PC side interface.
51.why: The relay command must be on the interface that receives PC-A's DHCPv6 messages, Gig0/0. On the wrong interface the router never hears the requests, so it can't forward them.

52.tip: Stateless = no state = no list of clients. Active clients stays 0.
52.why: In stateless DHCPv6 the server only gives extra info like DNS and doesn't hand out or track addresses. Since it keeps no client records, the active client count shows 0.

53.cue: Cisco-proprietary, only one router forwards IPv6
53.tip: One active forwarder + Cisco + IPv6 = HSRP for IPv6. Load sharing would be GLBP.
53.why: HSRP is Cisco's active/standby protocol where only the active router forwards. The IPv6 version is HSRP for IPv6. VRRP versions are open standards.

54.cue: nonproprietary IPv4-only election protocol, one master
54.tip: VRRP says MASTER. v2 = IPv4 only, v3 = IPv4 and IPv6.
54.why: VRRP is the open standard FHRP that elects one master router per group. Version 2 supports only IPv4, while VRRPv3 adds IPv6.

55.why: A /25 has 128 addresses, and removing network and broadcast leaves 126 usable. Reserving 10 for web servers leaves 116.

56.why: A /24 has 256 addresses, minus network and broadcast is 254 usable. Reserving 3 for printers leaves 251.

57.why: A /26 has 64 addresses, so 62 are usable after removing network and broadcast. Reserving 14 for file servers leaves 48.

58.why: A /24 has 254 usable host addresses (256 minus network and broadcast). Reserving 5 for printers leaves 249.

59.tip: Open standard + IPv4 only = VRRPv2. VRRPv3 scales better and does IPv6.
59.why: VRRPv2 is the open standard election protocol for IPv4 only. It's described as less scalable than VRRPv3. GLBP is Cisco-only and IRDP isn't an election protocol.

60.why: A /26 has 64 addresses and 62 usable hosts. Reserving 18 for access points leaves 44 for other hosts.

61.why: A /24 gives 254 usable addresses after removing network and broadcast. Reserving 3 for servers leaves 251.

62.why: A /24 gives 254 usable addresses. Reserving 6 for servers leaves 248 for other hosts.

63.why: A /25 has 128 addresses, so 126 are usable. Reserving 12 for web servers leaves 114.

64.tip: Renew early, renew direct: a unicast REQUEST to the server you already know.
64.why: Before the lease runs out, the client renews by sending a DHCPREQUEST straight (unicast) to the server that gave it the address. It doesn't need to discover servers again.
